01 / THE QUESTION

The business context.

When cellular infrastructure fails, emergency updates still need to move. Sending large multimedia payloads across multi-hop device networks strains bandwidth. The research explores whether compact representations can preserve useful meaning with less data to relay.

03 / THE APPROACH

From question to evidence.

01

Describe

Convert emergency content into compact semantic descriptors while addressing safety-critical fields.

02

Protect

Encrypt the payload for relay between devices.

03

Relay

Explore device-to-device transmission, including a controlled real-device payload test and a 250-node mesh simulation.

04

Reconstruct

Reconstruct meaning-equivalent artifacts and evaluate fidelity, structural similarity, hallucination, compression, and throughput.

04 / WHAT I LEARNED

The useful part of the analysis.

01

Multiple forms of evaluation

The paper evaluates reconstruction on 236 disaster-related images, tests relay payload transmission, and simulates packet loss in a 250-node network.

02

Trade-offs remain central

The work investigates compression and relay throughput alongside semantic fidelity and reconstruction risks.

03

A research contribution

Published at ITC 2026 as joint work with co-authors. The repository provides the research materials and attribution.

Communication resilience is about preserving useful meaning—not merely moving more bytes.

05 / SCOPE & LIMITATIONS

What the evidence does—and doesn’t—say.

This is a research-stage architecture, not a deployed emergency communication service. Further work includes outdoor mobility trials, device energy measurements, OS-level implementation, and safety-critical reconstruction benchmarking.
